description: We are a student team participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge and working on Flame in Freefall. We are interested in exploring how AI, data analysis, and visualization can help extract useful fire-safety insights from microgravity combustion data. Our goal is to build a clear, useful prototype using NASA data during the hackathon.
summary: Soraine connects an interactive 3D material lab with NASA combustion research. Users select familiar objects from a shelf, bring samples to a workbench, and open source-linked evidence to compare materials across Earth, microgravity, lunar and Martian gravity contexts. Our shared BigQuery collection preserves pressure, oxygen, airflow, specimen details and evidence types. The scene makes the topic approachable; the research browser lets students, educators and aerospace researchers check what the evidence supports. Schematic reactions remain separate from measured and model-derived results. Soraine supports research exploration and fire-safety education for spacecraft and pressurized habitats, rather than certifying materials or predicting exact fires.
details:
SORAINE is a virtual laboratory and research dashboard designed to help people explore NASA's combustion research through play. People with no scientific background can start with familiar objects and simple interactions, then look into the research behind what they see.

Users choose material objects from a shelf, bring them to a virtual workbench, and explore Earth, Moon, Mars, and orbital gravity settings. They can control oxygen delivery, observe individual sample states, and open related research. The aim is to give people a reason to ask how fire behaves in space and why those differences matter for crew safety.

The research dashboard adds the detail needed to investigate those questions. Its backend, built on Google BigQuery and Cloud Run, lets users compare published oxygen limits, search evidence, and follow citations to NASA sources. Each measurement retains its material, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, gravity conditions, and test method so readers can judge whether two results are comparable.

An Original Data view provides records from six NASA CSV collections. It preserves the original field names, values, blanks, approximations, and notes, including run logs and test configurations. These records remain separate from published paper results. The interface also distinguishes model estimates from experimental findings and leaves missing information visible.

The planetary settings introduce gravity contexts, while the research concerns controlled experimental atmospheres relevant to spacecraft and pressurized habitats. Scene animations explain concepts; they do not predict an actual habitat fire. Visitors can use the laboratory to learn through exploration, while students, educators, and researchers can examine the conditions and sources behind each comparison.

TEAM SI ASSISTANCE AND DEVELOPMENT LOG

Soraine: Team SI Assistance and Development Log

Challenge: Flame in Freefall, NASA Space Apps 2026

Team: Hogan, Ethan, Tony and Johnson

Coverage: Official build period beginning November 14, 2026 at 9:00 a.m. Eastern, through the final submission work on November 15, 2026. Pre-event planning is excluded. Entries are grouped by day or work session when an exact time was not recorded.

Final project: https://soraine-flame-lab.vercel.app/

Team repository: https://github.com/TonySama-BoiledCabbage/Soraine_Nasa-Space-App

How the team used SI

We used SI to help organize research, develop and debug software, explore visual directions, prepare documentation and refine the presentation. Hogan worked with OpenAI Codex, Ethan worked with Claude, and Tony's process record describes Claude and Codex assistance across the shared implementation. Johnson's record covers research documentation, pitch development and media-production briefs; the team also used Gemini for a design prompt. Higgsfield supported visual reference and animation experiments. NotebookLM and CapCut were included in presentation-production briefs, rather than treated as proof that every proposed output was generated or used.

The team supplied the concept, sketches, references, scientific priorities and feedback, chose which outputs to keep, and approved releases. SI helped implement those decisions. We did not use generated imagery as experimental evidence or create new NASA measurements. Extracted results retain their sources, units, test conditions and evidence categories.

This log combines the four members' supplied records. Earlier prototypes are included as development history; their features should not all be read as features of the final application. The final submission URL above replaces the earlier soraine.vercel.app address.

Tony: Final scene, research interface and technical process

Tony's supplied process document records the shared development work rather than individual timed prompts. It credits Claude and Codex assistance with research organization, implementation planning, code, asset integration and verification. Human decisions included the research question, interaction sketches, model selection, scientific boundaries and integration choices.

The documented iterations connected a searchable research collection to a 3D material shelf, familiar product objects, quantities, a hand-carried basket and workbench inspection. The team added independent sample states and inspection pause so copies of one material could be examined separately. Camera priorities and the research detail view were refined in the final application.

The research pipeline uses Python and SQL to prepare linked measurements, experiment contexts, source records and supporting statements. Shared public routes deliver research, original data and material-search results through Cloud Run and BigQuery. Cached responses and saved snapshots retain delivery labels. Retrieval ordering is a search aid, not a validated material-safety ranking.

Tony's final process record describes schematic heat, charring and gloss cues. These differ from the earlier reaction implementation logged above and remain illustrative. It also records instability in some microgravity basket-unloading cases. Passing data-contract or reaction checks do not establish that the full basket workflow or physical model is validated.

These entries describe SI assistance with preparation and documentation. They do not by themselves establish the duration, publication or contents of the final exported video. Mentor comments informed revisions; no endorsement of scientific predictive accuracy is claimed.

Scientific boundaries and verification

The research collection contains 59 measurement records, including published summaries, fits and model-derived results, not 59 independent experiments. Its 307 source entries are a catalogue, not a claim that 307 papers were fully reviewed. The 381 original CSV rows include configurations, logs, references and notes. They are not interchangeable with oxygen-extinction thresholds.

Gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure and airflow are separate experimental conditions. A Moon or Mars scene is not evidence that an ordinary flame burns in the unmodified outdoor atmosphere. The fire-safety interpretation concerns controlled experiments and habitable environments with supplied atmosphere. Familiar shelf objects are entry points to research materials, not necessarily the specimens tested by NASA.

The 3D reactions are schematic. They do not calculate certified flammability, real specimen temperature or exact habitat fire behavior. Missing evidence does not mean a material is safe. Automated tests, source comparisons and browser checks support software and data integrity; they do not replace combustion experiments, formal usability studies or real-device performance testing.
